Try to build harmony between species and biomes, even if this means sacrificing parts of your sanctuary by covering them with new ones, always more beautiful… The goal of Nimalia is to conceive the best Animal Sanctuary along 5 rounds. Each and every turn, players will have to select the animal territories they are going to place, by drafting them (picking a card among their hand of 3 cards, and passing along the rest of them). Each card they place will have to cover a part of their existing animal reserve. At the end of each round, points will be allocated to players regarding how efficiently they fulfilled objectives. Objective cards will be randomly chosen for each game. Every round will be considering only some of those objectives. So players will have to design their animal sanctuary regarding the ongoing objectives, but also anticipating the next upcoming objectives. Of course, at the end of the 5 rounds, the player that earned the more points will win the game. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary The game lasts 5 rounds, and each round comprises 3 phases: • Build Your Reserve • Calculate Your Points • Finish the Round Contents 1 Build Reserve 2 Calculate Points 3 Finish Round 4 End of the game Build Reserve At the beginning of each round, each player draws 3 Animal cards. Then, you simultaneously place one of these cards in front of you, to create and modify your reserve. Next, you pass the 2 remaining cards to your left neighbor (in rounds 1, 3, and 5) or your right neighbor (in rounds 2 and 4). Repeat this procedure with the 2 cards you just received from your neighbor, and then place the final card. When you modify your reserve, you must respect the following rules: • Each card you place must cover at least one space of your existing reserve (this does not apply to the very first card you place). • The entirety of your reserve must fit within a 6-space×6-space area. • You are not allowed to tuck a card under cards already in your reserve. Calculate Points After placing all three cards, everyone scores their points by moving their tokens on the score track. You score points according to the different objective cards that are in effect this round (as indicated by the Round card). • Round 1: the blue and green cards. • Round 2: the green and yellow cards. • Round 3: the blue and red cards. • Round 4: the green, yellow and red cards. • Round 5: the blue, red and yellow cards. If there is a tie on a red objective, all of the tied players receive (or lose) the points! If the tie is for 1st place, 2nd place is not awarded. Finish Round If this was not the 5th round, advance the Round Counter token to the number of the next round, and start a new round. Don’t forget to flip the round Counter token to know in which direction you should pass your cards this round. Otherwise, this is the end of the game (see other side). End of the game At the end of the 5th round, the player with the most points wins. If it’s a tie, the tied player with the most animals of the same type in their reserve wins. [Rating: 2/10] My family hated this game. Found the puzzle frustrating. Having to cover up things and having to give up good cards to get bad ones was no fun. Passing cards that stink for your layout to the next player felt WAY TOO MEAN. And my youngest struggled with the 6x6 grid restriction. Maybe this will work for adults - but not for the family. Rating a 2 for the family. Rating 5.5 for adults --- so 4 is an average score. Really  disappointed by this game. But I think I have learned... that closed drafting is just not a mechanism that for the most part - does not work for me. Update: I tried this solo,

[Rating: 2/10] This was not for me. On our first play, we had contradictory goals, which was a bummer. I did like how the goals changed round-to-round, but all of the goals were far too easy to achieve. In other words, we only had to care about the 3 animals who concerned the goals, other animals didn't matter at all. Placement was trivial and it rarely took more than ten seconds to choose which card we'd take next. Maybe a better combination of goals save this, but why bother? [Rating: 2/10] Pick-and-pass drafting is one of my pet hates and this game is basically built around it, so it was never going to be a favourite.  There's some interest added by the set of scoring conditions which fluctuate in significance as the game goes on as they each score at the end of particular rounds, which I think does make the decision-space potentially more interesting than 7 Wonders et al, however the cost for that is that we're all solving a personal player board puzzle, which isn't great either.

[Rating: 3.6/10] This barely felt like a game. Every turn I found it obvious which card to keep and which to pass on and I feel there was very little challenge building your tableau. On that basis, who wins feels very much luck based, as long as no silly mistakes are made. It's a shame because I feel it's a genre I like a lot but maybe it's just more of a kids or entry level game but BGG doesn't seem to suggest it as primarily being a kids game so my expectations were higher.
